# plughost

> Rust library for offline and realtime VST3, Audio Unit, and CLAP hosting. Applications
> control plugin chains through isolated helper processes and supply their own audio and
> timeline.

This reference describes plughost 0.2.0 and requires Rust 1.92 or newer. It covers the
public application API, its native limitations, and the helper an application must ship.
Use the typed API documentation for complete signatures.

## Entry points

- [Installation and stereo render example](README.md)
- [Application API](https://docs.rs/plughost/0.2.0/plughost/)
- [Shared types and render API](https://docs.rs/plughost-core/0.2.0/plughost_core/)
- [In-process formats](https://docs.rs/plughost-formats/0.2.0/plughost_formats/)
- [Helper runtime](https://docs.rs/plughost-helper/0.2.0/plughost_helper/)
- [Application exports](crates/plughost/src/lib.rs)
- [Changes](CHANGELOG.md)

## Dependencies and deployment

The application depends on `plughost = "=0.2.0"`. A separate executable depends on
`plughost-helper = "=0.2.0"` and calls `plughost_helper::run()` from `main`, returning
`std::process::ExitCode`. Ship that executable with the application and pass its path to
`Scanner::new` and `Chain::spawn`. The library supplies the helper's command-line arguments
and IPC handshake. Keep application and helper versions matched; the internal helper protocol
is 34, and an application and a helper with different protocol versions fail the handshake with
`Error::ProtocolVersion`, which carries both versions.

Supported targets are `aarch64-apple-darwin`, on macOS 15 or newer, and
`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. Audio Units are macOS-only. The helper and loaded plugin must use the same architecture. Intel Macs,
Rosetta, Linux, and cross-architecture bridges are outside the supported targets.

On macOS the helper is a background `LSUIElement` application, signed with Hardened Runtime
and the `disable-library-validation` and `allow-unsigned-executable-memory` entitlements.
Pass the executable inside `Contents/MacOS`, not the `.app` directory. The repository's
[packaging script](scripts/macos/package-app.sh)
uses ad-hoc signing for local development; the distributing application owns its production
signing and notarization. On Windows pass the helper `.exe` path.

`plughost-formats` loads native code in the calling process, so its loaders are `unsafe fn`:
`plughost_formats::load(&plugin_ref, &host)`, `vst3::Module::load` and `load_with_host`,
`clap::Entry::load(bundle)` and `au::Plugin::new(class_id)`. Their safety condition is trusting
the plugin's code with the whole process, or running it in a process of its own, as plughost's
helper does. Using a loaded plugin is safe, apart from `open_editor`, which takes a raw parent
view: `vst3::Plugin::new(&module, ..)`, `clap::Plugin::new(&entry, ..)`, `entry.classes()`,
`clap::preset_providers(&entry, ..)` and `clap::discover_presets(&entry, ..)` take the loaded
module, which stays loaded while they or a plugin created from it need it. Its default features
are `vst3`, `au`, and `clap`; direct users can disable defaults and select formats.
`HostedPlugin` and `BlockProcessor` are sealed: the format plugins and their processors
implement them, and an application calls them; `render::Process` and `AudioThread` stay open for
applications to implement. `Sample` is sealed too, implemented by `f32` and `f64` alone.
`HostedPlugin::set_editor_scale` exists on every platform and returns `None` where an editor
takes no explicit scale (outside Windows, always). Native lifecycle/controller/editor calls
normally belong on the main thread, with the OS event loop running. A plugin's
`BlockProcessor` processes it from another thread; an owner that
does gives the plugin an `AudioThread` with `HostedPlugin::set_audio_thread`, and the
audio-thread calls the plugin needs between blocks (delivering edits to a prepared VST3
processor, CLAP `params.flush` while active, `reset` and `stop_processing`) run there instead
of on the calling thread. `plughost-helper` uses all format features and owns these threads
and loops: it processes blocks on a thread of its own, which also makes those calls. Use
`plughost` for application-level crash isolation.

## Discovery

Construct `Scanner::new(helper_path, cache_path)`. Both arguments are `&Path`. The default
search covers standard VST3/CLAP directories, `CLAP_PATH`, and the macOS Audio Unit registry.
Use `.directories(Vec<PathBuf>)` to choose bundle directories explicitly. Native inspection
is serial by default; `.jobs(n)` explicitly enables parallel loading (`0` selects `1`).
On macOS, Audio Unit registry enumeration uses one of those worker slots and overlaps bundle
inspection when the limit exceeds one. The serial default queries the registry after bundles.
`.host(HostIdentity)` sets the identity native inspection presents to plugins, as
`Chain::spawn` does (default: `HostIdentity::default()`): VST3 factories receive it as their host
context, and CLAP inspection reads descriptors without a host. Cached native results are reused
whichever identity inspected them. An invalid identity fails `scan` and `retry` with
`Error::Input` (`InputError::HostIdentity`) before any helper starts.

Use `.policy(ScanPolicy)` for explicit selection. `ScanPolicy::default()` allows all items;
`ScanPolicy::new(ScanAction::Block)` allows only identities with an explicit Allow rule.
Add rules with `.bundle(path, ScanAction::Allow/Block)` or
`.audio_unit(class_id, ScanAction::Allow/Block)`. Last rule per identity wins. Bundle paths
must match discovered paths exactly; paths are not canonicalized. AU IDs ignore ASCII case.
Blocked bundles report `ScanOutcome::Blocked` without inspecting/loading the binary, preserving
cached entries and failure counts. Blocked AU classes are omitted from both progress events
and the catalog. The registry itself is still queried without instantiating plugins.
Rules apply to discovery, scan and retry. Allow does not reset automatic failure exclusion;
retry bypasses that exclusion but never bypasses Block. The caller owns/persists these rules,
separately from native cache results. They select scanner results, not permission to load a
PluginRef through Chain or the direct formats API.

`scanner.discover()` returns a `Catalog` without loading bundle code or writing the cache.
It reads compatible binary headers, static VST3 `moduleinfo.json`, and unchanged native cache
results. Missing or malformed metadata yields `ScanOutcome::NotInspected`, not an automatic
native load. Cached native failures remain visible without being retried. Audio Unit registry
enumeration uses a helper without instantiating the units. Missing, unreadable, malformed,
or incompatible caches are treated as empty by `discover` and `discover_controlled`.

`scanner.scan(&progress)` inspects native classes and accepts a `Sync` callback receiving
`&BundleScan`. With multiple jobs it can be called concurrently. Static metadata never
substitutes for native inspection, but unchanged native results can be reused from cache.
Each result includes its source, outcome, failure count,
and exclusion state. `Catalog::plugins()` returns `(PluginRef, &PluginInfo)` entries, and
`BundleScan::plugins()` those of one bundle, such as a `retry` result.

A plugin class's identity is a `PluginId`: its `PluginFormat` and `ClassId`, independent of
where it is installed. `ClassId` is canonical, so IDs written in another case are the same class:
VST3 class IDs (32 hexadecimal digits, as `.vstpreset` files use) and Audio Unit IDs (type,
subtype and manufacturer as 24 hexadecimal digits) are kept in upper case, CLAP IDs as given.
`PluginInfo::id` and `PluginRef::id()` give it, and the catalog lists one entry per `PluginId`,
from the highest priority directory that has it. Persist the `PluginId` (it supports serde, as a
`format` of `"vst3"`, `"audio-unit"` or `"clap"` and a `class_id`), not a path, and find the
installed class with `Catalog::resolve(&id)`, which returns the `PluginRef` to load or `None`.
A `PluginRef` is the identity and the location: build it with `PluginRef::vst3(bundle, class_id)`,
`PluginRef::clap(bundle, class_id)` or `PluginRef::audio_unit(class_id)`, or take discovered
values; Audio Units are found in the system registry, without a bundle.
Bundle and preset paths must be valid Unicode. `Chain::spawn`, `load_discovered_preset`,
`preset_providers` and `discover_presets` reject unrepresentable paths with
`InputError::PathEncoding` before sending them to a helper, and `discover_presets` rejects a
target `PresetDiscoveryTarget::validate` refuses (an empty, NUL-containing or oversized provider
ID, or a relative or oversized file location) with `InputError::PresetDiscoveryTarget`. Scans report only that bundle as
`Failed(InvalidInput)`, leave it uncached and continue with the other bundles.

Neither metadata discovery nor native class inspection proves that instantiation,
preparation, or processing will succeed. Audio Units are enumerated from the registry in
both paths. Cache schema 3 contains native bundle results with the classes' `PluginId`; earlier caches are
invalidated and their bundles inspected again.
Cache compatibility depends on the schema and architecture, not the plughost version.
Matching fingerprints reuse the native result before reading binary headers or static metadata.
The default scan stall timeout is 30 seconds. Two consecutive failures of an unchanged
bundle exclude it from automatic loading; the scan that reaches the limit already reports
`excluded`. `Scanner::retry(path)` bypasses exclusion and
uses a 24-hour stall timeout for interactive loading.
Failures before the helper receives its scan request, including startup and handshake errors,
do not replace cached native results or increase a bundle's failure count.

Bundle cache fingerprints cover the executable, Contents/Info.plist and
Contents/Resources/moduleinfo.json paths, sizes and modification times. Changes, addition or
removal of these files invalidate results; changing a failed binary resets its failure count.
This is metadata-based invalidation, not content hashing of every resource in a bundle.
AU registry results are never cached and are queried for every invocation. Enumeration includes
effects, MIDI-controlled audio effects, instruments and MIDI-only processors; being listed does
not imply that their event-processing capabilities are implemented.

VST3 metadata is parsed as JSON5, as the VST3 SDK does; malformed files and documents
exceeding 64 nested value levels are ignored. Only audio module classes are listed; compatibility mappings and snapshots
are not interpreted. Native factory enumeration supplies IPluginFactory3::setHostContext
when supported, with a live IHostApplication retained for the module lifetime. Direct
`Module::load_with_host(path, &HostIdentity)` and the generic formats loader use the caller's
identity; `Module::load` uses the default plughost identity, and scan helpers use the
`Scanner`'s. Instance initialization
still receives its own host context. A factory that ignores the optional context remains usable.

Native inspection may show plugin license dialogs. `scan_controlled(&control, &events)`,
`discover_controlled(&control, &events)` and `retry_controlled(path, &control, &events)`
accept a `ScanControl::default()` and a `Sync` callback receiving `&ScanEvent`. Retain a
clone of the control on the UI/control thread and call `cancel()` to stop all operations
using it. Cancellation is permanent for that control; use a new one for an independent run.

`ScanEvent::Progress { item, stage }` identifies `ScanTarget::Bundle(path)` or `AudioUnits`
and the Inspecting/StartingHelper/Loading/ModuleLoaded/ClassFound stage. Clone and retain
`item`, then call `item.skip()` to stop only that item. Late skip requests cannot affect
the next item, including a later scan of the same path. `BundleFinished` and
`AudioUnitsFinished` carry completed outcomes. Callbacks run on scanner workers, can overlap
with explicit parallelism, and must return promptly; dispatch UI work from them.

Cancellation stops new admissions, interrupts helper startup/handshake/response supervision,
and reaps active helpers before the scan call returns. Already admitted work may briefly
start before its next stop check. Directory traversal checks between filesystem entries;
blocking OS filesystem calls and caller callbacks cannot be interrupted. `Cancelled` and
`Skipped` are distinct outcomes, preserve old cache entries/counts, and are never cached as
plugin failures. Unadmitted items are absent from the returned catalog. Native processing
is terminated with its helper; no plugin cooperation or license diagnosis is required.

Native scans/retries save each changed bundle result before its `BundleFinished` notification.
An interrupted scan retains completed results and existing entries for unprocessed paths.
Cancelled/skipped items and unchanged cache hits do not rewrite the snapshot; if nothing has
been saved, cancellation need not create a cache JSON file. Use `retry_controlled` for chosen
paths after cancellation; it preserves other entries. A native scan first drops the entries of
bundles that are no longer on disk under a scanned directory that exists. A directory that is
missing, such as one on a disconnected volume, keeps its entries for when it returns, and an
entry with failures keeps its count and exclusion until a retry; a retry changes only the
retried path's entry. A link to a bundle or folder on a disconnected volume keeps its entries.
ClassFound notifications are provisional
until the bundle finishes. No failure or timeout is interpreted as a license diagnosis.

The writer publishes each snapshot as compact JSON through a unique sibling temporary file and
atomic replacement. The final snapshot is synchronized to stable storage once, when the scan or
retry ends (Unix also synchronizes the containing directory); after a power loss mid-scan the
cache can read as empty and is rebuilt. Native scan/retry writers treat missing, malformed,
and incompatible caches as empty, but return `Error::Cache` on existing-file read failures,
write/sync failures, or lock errors. Discovery tolerates read failures as described above.
A mid-scan save failure stops admissions and reaps active helpers. The caller's
ScanControl is not marked cancelled by an internal cache error. Results saved earlier remain
available, while the result whose save failed is not announced as completed. A final sync
failure can occur after a complete replacement has become visible; it is still an error.

One native scan/retry writer can use a cache path at a time. A competing writer gets
`Error::Cache` with `io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock`, without loading plugins or waiting for the
first scan. The adjacent `<cache filename>.lock` file is intentionally retained; its OS lock
is released when the writer closes or its process exits. Discovery reads snapshots without
acquiring that lock and never writes the cache. A killed writer may leave an unpublished
`.plughost-cache-*` temporary, which is never read as a cache. Process interruption is covered;
power-loss durability and network filesystem behavior are not guaranteed. Render cancellation
is independent of scan cancellation.

## Chains and capability queries

`Chain::spawn(helper, slots, &options)` starts one helper for a nonempty slice of `ChainSlot`,
in chain order. Slots are zero-based indices in that slice. A `ChainSlot` is a `PluginRef`
(`ChainSlot::new(plugin)` or `plugin.into()`) with an optional `StatePurpose::Project` state
(`.with_state(state)`) and native bypass (`.with_bypass(enabled)`): each plugin loads, restores
its state in place on that instance, which loads it once, and takes its bypass before the call
returns. A state of another plugin class fails with `FailureKind::StateMismatch` for its slot.
`SpawnOptions` (`SpawnOptions::default()` or `SpawnOptions::new(host, timeouts)`) holds the
`HostIdentity`, the calling application's identity, which recovered chains keep, and the
`Timeouts`.
`Timeouts` separates load, control, and block-processing operations. Defaults are 300,
60, and 10 seconds respectively; start from `Timeouts::default()` and set the fields to change.
A duration too long to end at a representable instant, such as `Duration::MAX`, waits without a
deadline.
Loading, restoring state, importing or loading a preset, selecting a factory preset, opening
an editor, preparing one slot again (`reprepare_slot`), and preparing an already configured
chain again use the load timeout. Initial preparation, reset, `resync_realtime`, saving state,
preset inspection/export, and parameter/control queries use the control timeout.
`recover_realtime` uses the load timeout for loading the plugins and restoring their states and
the control timeout for the rest. Processing one block uses the process timeout. A timeout is how
long the helper may go without responding: loading a chain and preparing an already configured
chain again go through the plugins one at a time, and each plugin that finishes renews the load
timeout for the next, so the timeout bounds each plugin rather than the whole chain. Scan stall
timeouts are configured separately on `Scanner`; they do not use `Timeouts`.

Types that later versions extend are `#[non_exhaustive]`: the enums `Layout`, `PluginFormat`,
`PluginKind`, `EventData`, `ExpressionKind`, `TailPolicy`, `Tail`, `RenderStatus`, `StatePurpose`,
`PresetMetadata`, `FactoryPresetId`, `ParameterEvent`, `DiagnosticSeverity`, `FailureKind`,
`InputError`, `RenderError`, `PresetSearchError`, `Error`, `ScanOutcome`, `Source`, `ScanTarget`,
`ScanStage`, `ScanEvent`, `Fallback`, `FallbackReason`, `RealtimeOutput`, `Message`,
`AudioBusRole`, `AudioDirection`, `AudioSource`, `EventSource`, `ChannelAdaptation`, `Support`,
`SampleFormat`, `ProcessMode`, `SessionState`, `PresetLocation`, `EditorRequest` and the formats
crate's `EditorView` need a wildcard arm in a `match`. `ScanAction` is exhaustive.
The structs `Event`, `Note`, `NoteExpression`, `RenderOptions`, `Transport`, `BlockContext`,
`Timeouts`,
`PluginInfo`, `EventPortInfo`, `AudioBusInfo`, `Capabilities`, `CapabilityReport`,
`PluginTiming`, `ParameterInfo`, `ParameterFlags`, `ParameterDetails`, `FactoryPreset`,
`PresetInfo` and `RealtimeConfig` are built with their `new` or `default` constructors and then
their public fields, not struct literals. So are the inputs an application writes:
`RoutedChainConfig::new(sample_rate, max_block_size, sample_format, inputs, slots)` with
`with_mode` and `with_event_inputs`, `SlotAudioConfig::new(inputs, outputs)` with
`with_configuration` and `with_events`, `AudioConfig::new(sample_rate, max_block_size,
sample_format, inputs, outputs)` likewise, `AudioBusConfig::new(id, layout, active)`,
`AudioInputRoute::new(bus, source)` with `with_adaptation`, `SlotEventConfig::new`,
`EventInputRoute::new`, `EventConfig::new`, `ProcessConfig::new(sample_rate, max_block_size,
sample_format, input, output)` with `with_mode`, `HostIdentity::new(name, vendor, version)`,
`ParameterChange::new(id, offset, value)`, `AutomationEvent::new(slot, change)`,
`RenderInput::new(audio, frames, events)` with `with_schedule`, `RenderSchedule::default()` with
`with_transport`, `with_automation` and `with_ramps`, `AutomationRamp::new`,
`TransportChange::new`, `TimeSignature::new`, `LoopRegion::new`, `BarPosition::new`,
`PresetDirectory::new`, `PresetFile::new`, `PresetDiscoveryTarget::new` and
`DiscoveredPreset::new(location)`. Modes default to `ProcessMode::Offline`, a slot keeps its
named configuration and leaves its event ports inactive, and a route matches layouts exactly.
`Rendered`, `RenderProgress`, `Delivery`,
`ChainSnapshot`, `RealtimeStatus`, `RealtimeFailure`, `ChangeBatch`, `SlotChange`, `Catalog`,
`BundleScan`, `Failure`, `Diagnostic`, `DiagnosticBatch`, `ParameterGroup`, `ParameterChoice`,
`ParameterChoicePage`, `ParameterEventBatch`, `AudioConfiguration`, `BypassState`,
`DecodedPreset`, `vst3::Preset` and the preset discovery results (`PresetFileType`,
`PresetLocationInfo`, `PresetSoundpack`, `PresetProviderInfo`, `PresetPluginId`,
`PresetDiscovery`, `PresetFileFailure`) are non-exhaustive output-only structs supplied by the
library; callers read their fields rather than construct them. CLAP preset discovery reports its
flags as `PresetFlags` (`FACTORY_CONTENT`, `USER_CONTENT`, `DEMO_CONTENT`, `FAVORITE`), keeping
bits later CLAP versions define.

`chain.plugins()` returns loaded plugin metadata. `chain.capabilities(slot)` returns a
`CapabilityReport` with native plugin evidence and isolated-host implementation support.
Both sides must support an operation. Treat `Support::Unknown` separately from
`Support::Unsupported`, and query again after configuration changes. Even a supported
operation can fail for a particular native configuration.

`Chain::prepare_audio(&RoutedChainConfig)` is the one preparation entry point.
Preparation rejects more than `MAX_AUDIO_BUSES` (64) buses or `MAX_AUDIO_CHANNELS` (512)
active channels per direction, including the chain’s external inputs.
`chain.main_bus_config(sample_rate, max_block_size, input, outputs)` builds the common
serial case: f32, `ProcessMode::Offline`, the chain input on the first slot's main input,
each slot's main output on the next slot's main input, and one output `Layout` per slot.
Instruments use `Layout::None` for their main input; auxiliary buses stay inactive. Change
fields such as `sample_format` or `mode` before preparing.
`ProcessMode::Realtime` only changes the mode reported to the plugin; rendering remains
offline and is not paced to wall-clock time. Prepare with it for a realtime endpoint (see
Realtime processing), which does not change the mode itself.

## Audio buses and precision

Call `audio_buses(slot)` and `audio_configurations(slot)` for native bus information.
An empty configuration list does not mean individually configurable buses are unavailable.
A CLAP plugin with configurations it cannot describe port by port (`audio-ports-config`
without `audio-ports-config-info`) fails `audio_configurations` with an unsupported error, and
one with more than 1,024 configurations, or more than `MAX_AUDIO_BUSES` ports in a direction of
one, with an audio metadata error.
An unknown speaker layout must not be inferred from its channel count.

`RoutedChainConfig` configures explicit routing and f32/f64 precision.
The configuration contains external input layouts and one `SlotAudioConfig` per plugin.
Each input route has an `AudioBusConfig`, an `AudioSource`, and `ChannelAdaptation`.
Sources select an external input bus, a previous slot's output bus, or silence. Native
bus IDs are scoped to direction and selected configuration. Omitted native buses are inactive.

Caller input channels are concatenated in external `config.inputs` order. Active native
output buses are concatenated in native bus-index order, not request-vector order. The
returned bus map describes the negotiated result. Channel adaptation must be explicit;
surround channels are never guessed, reordered, or automatically downmixed.

Layouts are none, mono, stereo, LCR, quad, 5.0, 5.1, 7.0, 7.1, 5.1.2, 5.1.4, 7.1.2, 7.1.4,
9.1.6, and first- to fourth-order ambisonics (ACN order, SN3D normalization). `Layout::ALL`
lists them, and each variant documents its one channel order, which is the order of its VST3
speaker bits: 7.1.4 is `L R C LFE Ls Rs Lss Rss Ltf Rtf Ltr Rtr`, with Ls and Rs as the rear
surrounds of layouts that also have side surrounds. Audio Unit buses use the matching system
channel layout tags (Atmos tags for 5.1.2 to 9.1.6, HOA ACN SN3D for ambisonics); where a tag
lists its speakers in another order, the host maps each native channel to its portable channel.
CLAP ports match a layout by their surround channel map or ambisonic format. Without a selected
configuration, a plugin with configurable audio ports is asked for the requested layouts during
preparation. CLAP has no wide speakers, so 9.1.6 is refused for CLAP plugins. AU processing is
f32 only. VST3/CLAP f64 requires native
plugin support. There is no resampler or implicit conversion between processing precisions.
Use `process_audio_f32` / `process_audio_f64` in the prepared precision.

Reconfiguring a prepared chain stages fresh instances and preserves the active chain on
returned native setup errors. A plugin that cannot save its state is prepared again in place
after the other slots are staged; a failure from then on leaves the chain unprepared, and blocks
fail with `FailureKind::NotPrepared` until it is prepared again. Initial preparation can partly
configure an unprepared native instance before failing. A native crash or timeout can terminate
the shared helper.

## Blocks, transport, and events

`Chain::process_audio_f32(context, input, output, automation, events, produced)` (or `_f64`)
processes one block of `events: &Events` and replaces `produced: &mut Events` with the chain's
output events; reuse an `Events::for_block()` for `produced`. All channel slices must have `context.frames` samples,
no more than the prepared maximum block size. `BlockContext::new(frames)` supplies frame
count without transport, and `.with_transport(transport)` adds one. The helper's reply is validated before it modifies output buffers.
Plugins process, reset and flush parameters with subnormal numbers flushed to zero, as inputs and
as results (MXCSR FTZ and DAZ on x86-64, FPCR.FZ on AArch64), in the helper and through
`plughost-formats`; out-of-process AUv3 extensions keep their own mode. Output differs from an
IEEE run only at subnormal level.
Automation points and events are fixed-size records: together they are limited to
`MAX_BLOCK_EVENTS` (4,096) per call across the chain, and system exclusive data, kept apart
from the records, to `MAX_BLOCK_SYSEX_BYTES` (64 KiB); excess input fails with
`InputError::EventCapacity` before DSP advances. Events that are not valid, not in offset order
or not inside the block fail with `InputError::Events`. Each slot's events, including those the
previous slot sends it, share that budget with its automation points; when a later slot cannot
take them, or a plugin sends more than a block allows, earlier slots have already processed the
block, so later blocks fail with `FailureKind::Processing` until `reset()`. Pending
control edits have a separate 4,096-entry budget (VST3 coalesces by parameter ID). Prepared
host event storage is reused. Native VST3 output-queue overflow blocks further processing until `reset` clears the failure.
External-input alignment storage is reserved during preparation and limited to
256 MiB per chain. A failed staged reservation preserves the old chain.

PCM and events use fixed shared-memory slots prepared for the selected precision and maximum
block size, in anonymous shared memory whose size neither process can change (a POSIX shared
memory object on macOS, a section backed by the paging file on Windows). Each generation has a separate 256 MiB shared-storage budget, plus local/native
buffers; re-preparation temporarily retains both generations. Control messages and completion
notifications use the socket. Processing still copies audio, allocates in other host paths,
and waits for the helper; shared memory does not make `Chain` real-time safe. An audio
callback uses a realtime endpoint instead (see Realtime processing).

`Transport` is a snapshot at the first sample of a block. `Transport::new(sample_position,
playing)` starts one; its optional timing fields remain unavailable when `None`, and the host
does not invent them. Beat positions use quarter notes.
The caller owns seeks and loop wrapping. Moving transport does not implicitly reset DSP.

`AutomationEvent::new(slot, change)` addresses a parameter independently of note routing.
`ParameterChange::new(id, offset, value)` holds the native parameter ID, sample offset, and
normalized value.
Values must be finite and in `0..=1`. Events are ordered by offset and lie inside the block.
Read-only or non-automatable targets are rejected when appropriate.

`Event { offset, port, data }` carries `EventData`: a MIDI 1.0 channel message
(`EventData::Midi`), a complete system exclusive message from `F0` to `F7`
(`EventData::SysEx`), a note on or off (`EventData::NoteOn` / `NoteOff` with a `Note`), or
the expression of single notes (`EventData::Expression` with a `NoteExpression`). Program
change and channel pressure have one data byte; the third byte is ignored, and `to_midi()`
gives it as 0.
`Event::new(offset, data)` builds any of them; `midi`, `note_on`, `note_off`,
`control_change` and `sysex` build MIDI 1.0 messages. `on_port(port)` selects one of the
chain's external event inputs and `at(offset)` moves the event. Offsets are block-relative for
direct processing and render-relative for rendering.

Events travel in an `Events`, which keeps fixed records with the system exclusive bytes of all
of them in one area, so a system exclusive message costs no allocation of its own. `Event<'a>` is
`Copy`: `EventData::SysEx(&'a [u8])` borrows bytes from the `Events` it was read from, or from the
caller (`Event::sysex(offset, &bytes)`). `push(event)` copies the event in; `iter()`, `get(index)`,
`len()`, `clear()` and collecting `Event`s build or read one, and it compares equal to a slice
or array of `Event`. `Events::new()` grows as needed, for a render's events;
`Events::for_block()` reserves one block's `MAX_BLOCK_EVENTS` events and
`MAX_BLOCK_SYSEX_BYTES` bytes, so pushing within them never allocates, and `push` beyond them
fails with `InputError::EventCapacity`; `Events::try_for_block()` returns a failed reservation
instead of aborting, and a clone of a block's `Events` reserves a block's room again.

A `Note` has a channel (0..=15), key (0..=127), velocity (0..=1; release velocity for a note
off) and an optional ID of at most `MAX_NOTE_ID` (`Note::new(channel, key, velocity)`,
`.with_id(id)`). IDs tell overlapping notes on one key apart; a note off or expression without
an ID addresses every note on its port, channel and key. A `NoteExpression` names its note the
same way and holds an `ExpressionKind` and a value that applies until the next value of that
expression: volume is linear gain 0..=4 (1 leaves the level), pan 0..=1 (0.5 center), tuning
-120..=120 semitones relative to the key, and vibrato, expression, brightness and pressure
0..=1. `EventData::to_midi()` gives the MIDI 1.0 form of MIDI messages, notes (velocity
rounded to 7 bits, a note on at least 1) and pressure (poly pressure). MIDI 2.0 is not
implemented.

`event_ports(slot)` lists a plugin's native event ports as `EventPortInfo` (native ID, index,
name, direction, and support for MIDI, system exclusive data, note expression and MPE). Note
expression support means notes keep their IDs and expressions arrive (CLAP ports with the CLAP
dialect, VST3 buses whose controller lists note expressions through INoteExpressionController);
MPE support is a CLAP port's MIDI dialect with MPE or an Audio Unit's `supportsMPE`, and VST3
declares none. `SlotAudioConfig::events` is a
`SlotEventConfig`: `inputs` route `EventSource::External { port }` or
`EventSource::Previous { port }` (a native output ID of the previous slot) to native input
ports, merging several routes to one port in offset order, and `outputs` names the native
output ports to collect. The last slot's collected outputs, in that order, are the chain's
event outputs; `RoutedChainConfig::event_inputs` counts its external event inputs, at most
`MAX_EVENT_PORTS` (16). `main_bus_config` routes external input 0 to the first slot's first
event input and each slot's first event output to the next slot's first event input.

A VST3 plugin without event input buses that maps MIDI controllers through IMidiMapping has
one input port that takes controller messages only. VST3 receives notes as note events with
their IDs, pressure as poly pressure, and the other expressions as note expression values of the
standard types, which reach a note by ID alone. A note off or such an expression without an ID
goes to each note on its key by that note's ID, so notes started without an ID take no
expression other than pressure. VST3 accepts at most 8,192 native events per block; a block whose
events expand beyond that limit is refused before that plugin processes it. In the first chain
slot this returns `Error::Input` with `InputError::EventCapacity`, and the caller can retry. In a
later slot it returns `Error::Operation` and requires `reset()`, because earlier slots have
already processed the block. CLAP ports that take the CLAP dialect receive notes, MIDI notes
and expressions as CLAP note and note expression events, and MIDI poly pressure as pressure when
they take no MIDI; other channel messages go as MIDI to ports that take MIDI or MIDI with MPE,
which receive notes and pressure in their MIDI 1.0 form where they have no CLAP dialect. System exclusive data goes only to ports that take MIDI. Audio Units take events on
port 0 only, in their MIDI 1.0 form; an AU MIDI event holds at most 65,535 bytes, so a longer
system exclusive message fails the block with `InputError::EventCapacity` before it is scheduled. An expression other than pressure has no MIDI 1.0 form and
does not reach MIDI-only ports. MPE is MIDI 1.0 on member channels: it is delivered as MIDI,
never converted into notes with IDs or note expressions.

Plugin output in a format's note events becomes notes and expressions: CLAP note and note
expression events, and VST3 notes, poly pressure and standard note expression values (named by
an ID the plugin's own note on gave). A CLAP note off or expression may name its note by ID
alone, and a VST3 note in the ID range VST3 reserves for plugins arrives, with its expressions,
without an ID. A VST3 note on with a tuning is followed by a tuning expression. MIDI output, legacy VST3 controller output and system exclusive data stay MIDI.
Events with no portable form are counted in diagnostics, not delivered (a CLAP note end, which
only reports a voice that ended, is neither); so are CLAP events whose header gives another size
than their type's. Output events a plugin places past the end of the
block land on its last frame. Audio Units send MIDI on one output port per MIDI output cable they
name. When a plugin produces more than one block's event budget, the block fails and
the chain refuses to process until `reset`, since events already delivered may be lost.

## Offline rendering

`render(&mut chain, input, frames, events, &options)` returns owned output channels,
removed latency, rendered tail length, and the chain's output events. Output event offsets
count from the start of the input and are not shifted by the removed latency. Input is one slice per input channel; each must
contain exactly `frames` samples. For an instrument, use empty input and explicitly select
`render::<f32, _>` or `render::<f64, _>` so the output precision can be inferred.

Rendering trims reported latency and appends a tail bounded by
`RenderOptions::max_tail_seconds` (`RenderOptions::new(tail, max_tail_seconds)`). The default
uses `TailPolicy::UntilSilence` with a
linear peak threshold of `1.585e-5`, a one-second hold, and a 30-second maximum tail.
Silence is judged on audio output only: output events do not count, and a chain without audio
outputs is silent from the end of the input, so its render stops one hold later.
`TailPolicy::Reported` uses the tail the chain reports when the render starts, capped by that
maximum; a tail reported during the render does not change its length.
`Rendered::status` says why a render ended: `RenderStatus::Complete`, or
`RenderStatus::TailLimit` when an `UntilSilence` tail reached the maximum before the output stayed
silent for the hold; a `RenderProgress` reports the same. A NaN or infinite output sample fails
the render with `RenderError::NonFiniteOutput { frame }` (`FailureKind::Processing`) at the first
output frame holding one, in any channel and whatever the tail policy; the failing block's output
is not delivered, and samples in the removed latency or after the silence hold are not checked.
For a session the frame counts from the output of that `push` or `finish`, and the session fails.
A maximum tail shorter than the hold always ends at `TailLimit`.

A chain's latency holds from one preparation or reset to the next, so rendering removes one
latency throughout. Each plugin's latency is read as it activates, on the helper's main thread.
A latency a plugin announces while it processes (VST3 `kLatencyChanged`, an Audio Unit's changed
latency property) does not stop processing or a render already running, and `take_changes()`
reports `PluginTiming::latency_changed` for its slot. `reprepare()` activates the plugins again
and applies it; VST3 plugins and Audio Units also take it on `reset()`, and, while a realtime
endpoint runs, on `resync_realtime()`. `reprepare_slot(slot)` does it for one slot, which a fresh
instance activates with its current latency. VST3 asks plugins to keep
the latency they were activated with until then, but many, like Audio Units, delay by the new
latency at once, so the chain's output is out of alignment until the application applies it. A
render does not start while a change is pending: it fails with `RenderError::LatencyNotApplied`
(`FailureKind::RestartRequired`) before processing anything. CLAP plugins change their latency by asking for a restart, which refuses processing until
the chain is prepared again. A plugin that asked to be prepared again (a CLAP restart, a VST3
`kIoChanged` or `kReloadComponent`) fails blocks with `FailureKind::RestartRequired` for its
slot until `reprepare()` or `reprepare_slot(slot)`; `reset()` keeps the request, and edits and
resets still apply. Tails follow
the plugins. Explicit timing reads, parameter/text edits, resets and render startup read current
native timing. Idle ticks and `take_changes()` poll VST3 and AU at most once per 100 ms after a
successful observation. A busy processing engine skips that poll and retries on a later tick;
the cached value can remain older while processing stays busy. CLAP polls read native tail only
after `tail_changed`, including a notification from a control-only flush; its processing thread
also reads tail after a block reporting that notification. Idle polls never wait for the native
engine lock or flush pending edits, and only changed observations are sent to the processing
thread. Processing uses cached latency. In-process hosts can use the optional
`HostedPlugin::poll_timing` for this opportunistic read; its default returns `None`, and
`HostedPlugin::timing` remains the fresh, fallible read.
A generic `render::Process` whose latency changes during a render still fails it with
`RenderError::LatencyChanged`; `Process::begin_render` lets it refuse a render before it starts.
An unprepared chain returns `NotPrepared` before input validation. `Process::validate_events`
checks destinations across the whole render before DSP advances; processors with configured
event ports implement it, including the chain and the direct VST3/CLAP renderers. Render sessions
perform the same check for each submitted segment.

`render_with_schedule` accepts a `RenderSchedule` containing automation points, ramps,
and transport changes. Offsets are render-relative. Transport changes and the combined
4,096-event budget delimit submitted blocks. Ramps expand into exact sample points for
one block at a time; native adapters perform any required internal subdivision.
`AutomationRamp` endpoints are inclusive and linear in normalized value; native metadata
quantizes discrete parameters. A single timestamp that exceeds the event budget is
rejected before rendering starts; equal-time events are never split across submissions.

`render_stream` takes `RenderInput`, a consumer of `Delivery { audio, events }` blocks, and a
cancellation callback. It
retains bounded output state instead of the complete result. Cancellation is checked
before submitted blocks, returns `RenderStatus::Cancelled`, and preserves already delivered
samples. It cannot interrupt a plugin already executing a native block; the processing
timeout bounds an unresponsive helper.

For offline throughput, choose `max_block_size` when preparing the chain. Larger supported
blocks reduce helper round trips for sparse events, while exact ramps can still reach the
event budget first. They also reserve more memory and increase the processing span between
cancellation checks. The renderer never silently increases that limit or submits ahead of
the next cancellation check. Silence trimming remains sample-based, although DSP may have
advanced through the remainder of the last submitted block. Check plugin output and
cancellation behavior at the chosen size; there is no universal optimal block size.

`RenderSession::new(&mut chain)` continues DSP across multiple `push` calls and one
`finish`, trimming latency and flushing the tail only once. Event and schedule offsets in
each `push` are relative to that segment. It does not reset the processor.
After cancellation or failure, drop the session and reset before starting an independent
render. A finished, cancelled, or failed session cannot accept further segments.

## Realtime processing

`chain.realtime_endpoint(&RealtimeConfig::new(quantum))` creates a `RealtimeEndpoint` for the
prepared chain. Every callback is one quantum of `quantum` frames, at most the prepared
`max_block_size`, in the prepared precision. `with_latency(1..=3)` sets the added latency in
quanta (default 1). `with_fallback(Fallback::Dry)` plays the input delayed by the whole latency
instead of silence while output is missing; it needs as many output as input channels. A new
endpoint replaces the previous one; preparing the chain again or dropping it retires the
endpoint for good, which then plays `FallbackReason::Stopped`; `recover_realtime` moves it to
another chain instead.

Move the endpoint to the audio callback's thread and call `process_audio_f32` or
`process_audio_f64` there once per callback, with the arguments of `Chain::process_audio_*`.
The call copies the input into shared memory, wakes the helper, and copies out the output of
the quantum submitted `latency` callbacks before; it never waits, locks, or allocates. It
returns `RealtimeOutput::Processed` or `RealtimeOutput::Fallback(reason)`: `Stopped`,
`Priming` (the first `latency` callbacks after a start, a resync or a recovery), `Missed` (the
helper had not completed that output), or `Resync`. A change of source ramps over one quantum:
into the fallback from the last sample played, and back to the output after a miss with a
crossfade. The first output after a start, a resync or a recovery plays as is, so without misses
the output is the offline output for blocks of one quantum, `latency * quantum` frames later. `produced` receives the output events, system
exclusive ones included, within the room it has reserved; pass an `Events::for_block()`. Events
beyond that room count as `dropped_events`. A missed output's audio is lost, but its events are
not: once the helper has completed it, they go out at offset 0, before the output's own, with
the next callback, so a note off it held still ends its note.
Invalid input is an error and starts a resync; wrong output buffers or precision are an error
and leave `output` unchanged. `endpoint.last_completion()` says how long the helper took for
the output just played. Drop the endpoint on a control thread. Call the endpoint once per
quantum's worth of time, as a device calls back: quanta processed in a burst find the previous
ones unfinished and play the fallback. Ask the device for callbacks of one quantum; cutting each
device callback into several quanta needs a latency of as many quanta as a callback holds.

From a control thread, `chain.start_realtime()` starts processing and returns the whole latency
in frames: the chain's latency plus `latency * quantum`. `chain.stop_realtime()` stops between
quanta; like `resync_realtime` and `recover_realtime`, it waits for a callback in progress, so
that none submits afterwards. `chain.realtime_status()` reports callbacks, processed and missed
outputs, overflows, callbacks of another size, failed quanta and the last failure, late
completions (quanta the helper completed more than `latency` quanta after their submission,
carried over a recovery), outputs played with a NaN or infinite sample (`non_finite_outputs`;
the device receives them as is, where rendering fails with `RenderError::NonFiniteOutput`),
dropped events, the latency, and `stalled`. A callback of another size, a full ring (the helper
fell `latency + 2` quanta behind), a failed quantum, or invalid input sets `resync`: the endpoint plays its fallback until
the application calls `chain.resync_realtime()` (or `recover_realtime`, below). It halts the
callbacks' submissions, which play `Resync` meanwhile, resets every plugin as `reset()` does,
ending held notes and applying an announced latency, and starts a new generation without
stopping the helper's worker: its quanta are numbered from 1 again and the first output plays as
is after `latency` priming callbacks, as after a start. It returns the whole latency in frames,
as `start_realtime` does, and changes nothing on a stopped endpoint. Stopping the endpoint,
calling `chain.reset()` and starting it again still works. The first callback of every new
generation (a start, a resync or a recovery) that returns `Ok` puts in `produced`, in place of
the output's events, a note off at offset 0 for each note earlier outputs started there and did
not end, in the form it started in; they count as `dropped_events` when `produced` cannot hold
them, and so does a note on beyond the 256 notes the endpoint tracks. A plugin whose reset does not return within the
control timeout fails the resync with `Error::TimedOut`.

`status.stalled` is the time since the helper's worker last completed a quantum (or since the
endpoint started or was recovered), while quanta the callback submitted are outstanding; it is
zero otherwise. It grows while a plugin hangs in its processing, and how long counts as a hang
is the application's choice. A crashed helper shows through `helper_monitor()` instead.
`chain.snapshot()` returns a `ChainSnapshot` whose `slots` hold each slot's plugin,
`StatePurpose::Project` state and native bypass (`None` where unavailable); it also works while
the endpoint runs, and plughost takes none by itself. After a crash or hang, call
`chain.recover_realtime(&snapshot.slots)`: it prepares a chain of those slots in a new helper as
`recover` does, installs a new ring there and moves the same
endpoint to the new chain, which starts the next generation (the callback goes on with the
`RealtimeEndpoint` it has, plays `Resync` from the call on and takes the new ring on its first
call of that generation). The application need not stop the endpoint first. Switch to the
returned chain and drop the old one; the old helper is not contacted, and a hung one only ever
sees the old shared memory. A failed recovery leaves the endpoint with the old chain, playing its
fallback with `resync` set, and retries nothing; without an endpoint the call returns
`Error::NotPrepared`. A new chain holds only what the slots hold.

While the endpoint runs, `reset`, `prepare_audio`, `reprepare`, `realtime_endpoint`,
`process_audio_*` and rendering fail with `Error::RealtimeRunning`; after `stop_realtime` they
work as before (`resync_realtime` resets under a running endpoint). Parameter edits and queries,
bus and capability queries, editors, bypass, `save_state`, `snapshot`, `export_preset`,
`take_changes`, and diagnostics go on, and so does replacing one slot: `restore_state`,
`import_preset`, `load_discovered_preset`, `select_factory_preset` and `reprepare_slot` swap a
fresh instance in between quanta (see below). Edits reach the plugins between quanta, and timing
changes arrive through `take_changes` instead of each edit's reply. A VST3 or CLAP restart
request is reported there while processing goes on with the current activation; call
`reprepare_slot(slot)` for that slot, or prepare the chain again after stopping, which a restart
that changes the slot's buses or event ports needs. `recover` is
allowed, but the new helper competes for the CPU.

The helper's worker runs with the time-constraint policy for the quantum in an audio workgroup
interval of its own on macOS, holding an activity that keeps App Nap away, and in the MMCSS
"Pro Audio" task on Windows; a refusal is reported in the diagnostics. Plugins' own code can
still allocate or lock; late completions count what that costs.

## Parameters, state, and presets

- `parameters(slot)` returns each `ParameterInfo` with its current normalized value as an
  `Option<f64>`. A CLAP plugin has at most its first 65,536 parameters listed; one that reports
  more gets a diagnostic.
- Every format treats the parameter values that `parameters` reads, and the ranges they come
  with, alike: a value outside its range is clamped into it, and one the plugin does not give (a
  CLAP `get_value` that fails, an `AudioUnitGetParameter` a v2 unit refuses), that is not finite,
  or whose range is not, is `None` rather than a value that looks like a real 0.
  `vst3::Plugin::parameter_value` is `None` for an unknown ID too. Values a plugin reports
  through its own edits and notifications outside their range are dropped, as before. A CLAP
  parameter whose range is not finite has no default, and edits and automation of a CLAP or
  Audio Unit parameter with such a range fail with a `FailureKind::Host` error.
- `parameter_details` returns native range endpoints and group information. Endpoints do
  not imply a linear mapping. A missing default is unavailable, not the current value.
- `parameter_choices` pages discrete native labels. Respect `PARAMETER_CHOICE_PAGE_SIZE`.
- `parameter_text`, `parameter_from_text`, `parameter_to_plain`, and
  `parameter_to_normalized` use the native conversion. Unsupported conversions return errors.
- `set_parameter` and `set_parameter_text` edit through native APIs and refresh prepared
  chain timing. An edit, or a `reset()`, that took effect succeeds even when a slot's timing
  cannot be read or planned afterwards: the chain keeps its last latency and tail, and the
  diagnostics record the failure. `bypass` / `set_bypass` use native bypass without host dry/wet substitution.
- `take_parameter_events` drains bounded value/gesture/metadata notifications. On overflow,
  cancel active gestures and requery metadata and values.

`save_state(slot, purpose)` returns an opaque `PluginState`; use `StatePurpose::Project` for
project persistence. Persist `state.to_bytes()` in application-owned storage and read it with
`PluginState::from_bytes`, which reads the bytes of every plughost version from 0.2.0 on (a
0.2 cannot read a state 0.1 serialized with serde; re-create it), needs no
plugin (a state of a plugin that is not installed is kept and written again unchanged), and
fails with `InputError::StateBytes` for bytes it cannot read, or `InputError::StateSize` for a
payload over `MAX_STATE_BYTES`, before allocating it. These bytes are plughost's own versioned
container of tagged sections (the identity, a VST3 component and controller kept apart, or the
single blob of the other formats), independent of the helper protocol; `PluginState` has no
serde form, nor do the other public types except `PluginId`: an application stores routing,
configurations and other settings in its own model. `id()` names the class that may restore it,
and `name()`, `vendor()` and `version()` the plugin that saved it, for display; they always come from the loaded plugin, also for an
imported preset. Restore only to the matching class with `restore_state(slot, &state,
purpose)`: the restore checks the `PluginId` and not the plugin version, so a state saved by
another version of the plugin restores and the plugin decides what to make of it.
`StatePurpose` distinguishes `Project`, `Preset`, and `Duplicate`. Native formats can reject
unsupported purposes.

`restore_state` stages a fresh instance, prepares it, and validates timing before replacing
the slot. Returned native failures preserve the active slot. A crash/timeout can still end
the helper. In a prepared chain, a fresh instance whose audio buses or event ports differ from
the ones the slot was prepared with, as a plugin whose ports depend on its state reports, fails
with `FailureKind::Configuration` and leaves the active slot; prepare the chain again to route
the new ones. Successful restore clears that slot's DSP history. It succeeds on a slot with a
pending restart request, which the replacement drops with the replaced instance (0.1.3 failed it
with `RestartRequired`); the same holds for the other replacements below. The slot keeps its native
bypass unless the state sets it, as a VST3 or CLAP state holding a bypass parameter can; preset
imports, discovered presets and factory presets do the same. Notes the replaced instance already
sent to later slots are not ended, so a note-producing plugin's replacement can leave them held;
`reset()` ends them, and `resync_realtime()` does while an endpoint runs. An open editor is recreated; reopening failures appear in diagnostics. State payloads are bounded by `MAX_STATE_BYTES`
(128 MiB across processor and controller payloads). A VST3 component or controller that
rejects its state fails the restore; a controller without state support does not.

`reprepare_slot(slot)` prepares one slot again on a fresh instance that holds the active one's
project state, replacing the slot as `restore_state` does. Use it for a restart request: the new
instance has no pending request, DSP history or notes of the replaced one. A plugin that cannot
save its state, such as an invalidated Audio Unit, fails the call and stays as it is; restore a
state the application saved instead. It requires a prepared chain. A restart that changes the
slot's active audio buses or event ports, as a VST3 `kIoChanged` can, fails it with
`FailureKind::Configuration` like any replacement; `reprepare()` (after stopping a realtime
endpoint) routes the new ones.

All of these replacements work while a realtime endpoint runs, and use the load timeout. The
helper stages the fresh instance on its main thread as it does offline, and the worker swaps it
in between quanta, deferring the new instance's restart requests as it does the old one's; the
stream goes on. A replacement that changes the chain's latency resynchronizes the endpoint right
after, as `resync_realtime()` does (which resets every plugin), because the endpoint does not go
on in a generation's timeline at another latency; the new latency is the one the resync
returns and `realtime_status` reports. A replacement that keeps the latency does not. The
replacement succeeds even when that resync does not complete: the endpoint then plays its
fallback with `resync` set, and a helper the resync found crashed or hung fails the next call,
as `helper_monitor()` reports.

`inspect_preset`, `export_preset`, and `import_preset` operate on native preset bytes;
the caller owns file I/O. `MAX_PRESET_BYTES` is 64 MiB. `factory_presets` and
`select_factory_preset` use native programs; VST3 selection requires preparation first.
`standard_preset_directories` and `discover_preset_files` find standard preset paths.
Discovery follows links and junctions, including a linked root, without revisiting link loops,
and skips unreadable entries; only an unreadable root is an error.
`preset_providers` and `discover_presets` run CLAP provider discovery in isolated helpers.
A directory location is crawled in one helper for the provider's declared file types, as preset
roots are; each `DiscoveredPreset` names its `location` (the plugin or the file it was found in),
and files the provider refused are listed in `failed_files`. A crash or timeout fails the whole
query. `load_discovered_preset` applies a preset's location/key on a fresh instance, also while
a realtime endpoint runs.
Discovery metadata alone does not prove a preset belongs to the currently loaded class.

The VST3 SDK's AUv3 samples pass parameter edits to their processor only while processing
and save the processor's state, so a state saved after an edit and before the next processed
block misses the edit. Do not assume every plugin implements all state, conversion, or preset
operations.

## Editors, errors, and recovery

`open_editor(slot)` creates a helper-owned native window; processing can continue while
it is open. Poll `editor_open(slot)` and call `close_editor(slot)` when appropriate.
A desktop session and the plugin's native editor implementation are required. A CLAP editor
that cannot draw inside the host window opens as its own floating window. The helper follows
plugin requests to open an editor (VST3 `requestOpenEditor`) and to show, hide or close an
open one (CLAP), so `editor_open` also changes without application calls; a hidden editor
stays open, and a request that fails to open an editor is reported in diagnostics. An Audio
Unit editor's window follows the size its view takes, except that an AUv3 running in its
extension process keeps the size it opened with: macOS does not pass later size changes of
such a view to the host. The editor window is not embedded in application windows. Opening
or showing an editor brings the helper to the front; on macOS the application that was
frontmost before is activated again when the helper's last window closes.

Match typed `Error` variants (`Error::Render` carries a `RenderError`, `Error::Input` an
`InputError`) or use `Error::kind()` for the shared `FailureKind`; do not parse display text.
Each input contract has one error: input that a render, a block or a configuration rejects is
`Error::Input`, never `Error::Render`, and audio buffers of the wrong channel count or length,
or a block longer than the prepared maximum, are `InputError::AudioBuffers`, and buffers of
another precision `InputError::AudioSampleFormat`.
`Error::source()`
exposes wrapped I/O, render, input and operation errors. `Display` gives the outer context;
format the source chain to include each cause once. `PresetSearchError`, `RenderError` and
`plughost_formats::Error` follow the same rule.

`plughost_formats::Error` is one opaque type for every format: `kind()` gives the
`FailureKind`, `input_error()` the rejected caller input, `format()` the format whose host
failed (none for rejected input), `native_code()` the VST3 `tresult` or Audio Unit `OSStatus` (an `NSError` code where
the call returns one), and `source()` the cause, such as the module loader's error or the
CLAP instance error. `failure()` flattens the chain into a transportable `Failure`. An Audio
Unit or a VST3 or CLAP class that is not found fails with `FailureKind::NotFound`.
After a timeout, protocol error or cancellation the
helper is terminated; later requests return `Error::Crashed` (`NotPrepared` for processing)
until the application recovers the chain. `Error::Crashed`, `Error::TimedOut` and `Error::Cancelled`
can include the last reported slot, which may be unavailable. Treat plugin failures as
recoverable application events.

`canceller()` returns a clonable `ChainCanceller` for the current helper generation. Its
`cancel()` terminates that helper from any thread and waits for it to exit, without waiting for
the chain; call it from application or control code, not an audio callback. It ends a call the
chain is blocked in, such as a plugin that does not return from restoring state, loading a
preset, opening its editor, preparing again or processing a block. Loading in `Chain::spawn`,
`recover` and `recover_realtime` is bounded by the load timeout instead, since the chain and its
canceller exist only once it is done. That call, or the chain's next call if none is blocked, returns
`Error::Cancelled` (`FailureKind::Cancelled`) with the slot the helper was calling; later calls
return `Error::Crashed` as after a timeout, until the application recovers the chain. A
recovered chain has its own canceller; cancelling a helper that already ended does nothing.

`reset()` clears DSP history while retaining settings. A reset that fails at one slot, after
earlier slots were reset, returns that slot's error and leaves the chain to be prepared again:
blocks fail with `FailureKind::NotPrepared` until `reprepare()` or `prepare_audio`. The reset of a
`resync_realtime` does the same, and the endpoint then plays its fallback.
`recover(&slots)` starts a separate chain of `slots` in a new helper with this chain's host
identity and timeouts, as `Chain::spawn` does, and prepares it with the saved audio
configuration. The original chain is not modified, so the application keeps a last known good
`snapshot()`, recovers from its `slots`, and replaces its chain only once recovery succeeds
(for the plugins' initial states, a `ChainSlot::from` each of `chain.references()`, the
references the chain loaded; the slots are not checked against them);
after a failure the original remains available for another attempt. Edits after the snapshot,
DSP history, open editors and unread diagnostics are not recovered. The snapshot records each
slot's native bypass, which a state holds only for a VST3 or CLAP bypass parameter and never for
an Audio Unit, and the recovered chain takes it. `recover_realtime` does the same for a chain
with a realtime endpoint (see Realtime processing); `recover` leaves the endpoint with the old
chain.
`reprepare()` reactivates the saved configuration once, and `reprepare_slot(slot)` one slot,
also while a realtime endpoint runs; repeated native restart requests remain visible to the
caller.

`helper_monitor()` returns a clonable `HelperMonitor` for the current helper generation. Its
`exit_status()` and `wait_for_exit(timeout)` observe the OS exit without IPC, including while
the chain is idle; wait from application or control code. Once the exit is observed,
`end_reason()` tells why the helper ended, which the later `Error::Crashed` results do not:
`FailureKind::Crashed` when it exited on its own (a crash, or a plugin ending the process),
`TimedOut`, `Protocol` or `Cancelled` when plughost terminated it for that reason, and `Closed`
when its chain shut it down. A recovered chain has its own monitor.
Helpers run in an application-owned macOS process group or Windows kill-on-close Job. Drop,
timeout, and scan cancellation terminate the helper and descendants that stay in that scope; a
helper also terminates its scope when the application exits or disconnects, even if a modal
dialog or stuck native call blocks its main thread. A panic in the helper aborts it, so the
application sees a crash of the slot the helper was calling rather than a timeout. An invalidated Audio Unit extension instance
fails later calls with `RestartRequired`; it is not recreated automatically.

`take_changes()` drains coalesced `PluginTiming` notifications per slot: the latency the plugin
was activated with, its tail, a restart request, and a pending latency change. `take_diagnostics()` drains
bounded structured plugin logs and helper failures. Unread helper-local diagnostics are lost
when that helper exits. Startup errors and arbitrary plugin stderr remain on stderr; plugin
stdout is discarded. Applications own recovery decisions and user-facing reporting.

## Development and examples

Repository examples are `plughost --example scan`, `plughost --example render` (an offline
batch with a state snapshot and recovery), `plughost --example realtime` (an audio callback
driving a realtime endpoint, with resynchronization and recovery), `plughost --example editor`,
`plughost-helper --example helper`, and `plughost-formats --example check`.
Run them through `cargo run -p <crate> --example <name> -- <arguments>`; each source file
lists its arguments. Native loading can show license dialogs, so select plugins explicitly.

The [README development section](README.md#development)
covers fixture/helper builds, tests, formatting, Clippy, API docs, and package verification.
Test plugins and build scripts live in the repository, outside published crate packages.
Keep crash/hang fixtures out of an application's normal plugin search directories.
